## Prompt Anatomy, Roles & Attention Placement

### Message roles and trust hierarchy

| Channel | Claude Messages API | Gemini / Vertex AI | What belongs here |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **System instruction** | Top-level `system` parameter | `system_instruction` in config | Role identity, non-negotiable behavioral rules, categorical criteria, global output conventions |
| **Reference & examples** | Early `user` content blocks or `system` blocks (with `cache_control`) | Cached prefix contents or early `user` parts | Domain glossary, schema normalization rules, `<examples>`, large source documents |
| **Untrusted payload** | Delimited block inside `user` (`<document>…</document>`) | Delimited part inside `user` | Raw customer messages, pull-request diffs, OCR text, web pages |
| **Task trigger** | Final lines of the `user` turn | Final part of the `user` turn | The specific question, target action, and reminder of edge-case rules |

### Structural delimiters and edge placement
* **Separate instructions from data:** wrap variable inputs in unambiguous tags such as `<document>`, `<diff>`, or `<customer_ticket>` rather than loose quotation marks. Clear boundaries stop multi-paragraph inputs from bleeding into your rules and make indirect prompt-injection instructions easier for the model to recognize as data.
* **Respect the U-shaped attention curve ("Lost in the Middle"):** across long prompts, recall is highest at the opening and closing edges of the window and weakest in the middle interior. Place large reference documents near the top (where they also form a stable cacheable prefix), put key findings summaries ahead of raw appendices, label sections with explicit headers, and state the exact task instructions and critical constraints at the very end.
* **Positive framing vs. hard negative boundaries:** frame style and workflow instructions positively (*"Write a 3-bullet summary citing section numbers"* outperforms *"Don't write long paragraphs or omit citations"*). Reserve strict negative directives (`NEVER`, `DO NOT`, `ONLY`) for safety gates, scope exclusions, and anti-fabrication rules (*"Return `null` when a date is absent; never estimate or infer missing dates"*).
* **Authoring checklist (Task · Context · Examples · Evaluate · Iterate):** define a concrete verb, role, and target audience (**Task**); supply the minimum situational facts and source boundaries needed (**Context**); attach 2–5 representative demonstrations (**Examples**); grade outputs on a labeled test set (**Evaluate**); and refine one variable per run (**Iterate**).

### XML tag disambiguation rules
Claude has no reserved tag vocabulary: any descriptive tag name works, provided it is used consistently. Gemini prompts benefit from the same discipline (clear prefixes or tags that separate instructions, context, and input).

| Rule | What goes wrong without it | Practice |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **One tag per content type** | Instructions, reference text, and live input blur together | Wrap each kind separately: `<instructions>`, `<context>`, `<examples>`, `<input>` |
| **Nest to express hierarchy** | The model cannot tell which passage a rule refers to | `<documents>` containing `<document index="2">` with inner `<source>` and `<content>` tags |
| **Refer to tags by name** | *"Use the document above"* is ambiguous once several blocks exist | *"Answer only from `<contract>`; apply tone rules from `<style_guide>`"* |
| **Keep names stable** | Renaming tags between prompt versions or examples confuses the model and breaks cached prefixes | Freeze tag names in the versioned template; change content, not structure |
| **Neutralize tag look-alikes in payloads** | Untrusted text containing `</input>` can fake the end of the data block | Escape or strip tag-like strings from the payload before insertion |
| **Name the output container** | Free-form replies mix commentary with the result | Ask for the result inside `<answer>` for human-facing text; use a JSON schema for machine consumers |

> **Retired pattern — assistant prefilling:** Older guides recommended ending a request with a partial `assistant` turn such as `{"role": "assistant", "content": "{"}` to force JSON output. Modern frontier models (Claude 4.6 and later) **reject assistant prefilling with HTTP 400**. Enforce structure with native JSON Schema decoding (`output_config.format` / `response_schema`) or strict tool calls instead.

---

## Explicit Criteria, Rubrics & False-Positive Control

### Why vague instructions and confidence prompts fail
In automated code review, compliance triage, and defect detection, **precision** (the share of flagged items that are genuinely actionable) governs whether engineers read or mute your system. Telling a model to *"be conservative"*, *"only flag high-confidence issues"*, or *"check that comments are accurate"* fails because it never defines the decision boundary—the model's internal threshold stays uncalibrated while noisy edge cases still slip through.

| Weak / vague phrasing | Failure mode in production | Explicit categorical specification |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| *"Check whether code comments are accurate"* | Flags minor wording preferences, TODOs, and abbreviated docstrings | *"Report a comment defect **only** when a comment's stated behavior directly contradicts the executable code path"* |
| *"Only report high-confidence bugs; be conservative"* | Model still emits stylistic nitpicks labeled `"high confidence"` | **Report:** null dereferences, auth bypasses, resource leaks, SQL/command injection. **Skip:** naming conventions, formatting, and idioms already established in the repository |
| *"Assign a severity of low, medium, or high"* | Severity labels drift across runs and files | Define each tier with explicit impact rules **plus one concrete code example per severity level** |

### Protecting developer trust in automated pipelines
* **One noisy category poisons every category:** if your PR reviewer is 92% accurate on security bugs but 35% accurate on "maintainability" warnings, developers stop reading *all* comments from the bot within days.
* **Measure precision per category, not only in aggregate:** track acceptance and dismissal rates separately for each rule family (`security`, `concurrency`, `null-safety`, `comment-drift`).
* **Disable noisy categories immediately while fixing them:** when a category produces excessive false positives, **turn that category off** in production right away to restore trust in the high-precision categories, then rewrite its criteria and few-shot contrast examples offline against an evaluation set before re-enabling it.

| Policy component | Role in the prompt contract | Concrete specification |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Report categories** | Enumerates the only defect classes eligible for comments | **`defect`** (runtime exceptions, off-by-one bounds, lost updates, unhandled promises); **`security`** (broken access checks, unsanitized shell/SQL/HTML sinks, secret exposure); **`comment_contradiction`** (a guarantee such as *"thread-safe"* or *"returns UTC"* violated by the code) |
| **Skip categories** | Explicitly suppresses high-noise style feedback | Formatting, variable naming, import ordering, missing docstrings, and established local repository idioms |
| **Severity rubric** | Anchors each severity tier to concrete runtime impact | **`critical`:** exploitable security flaw or guaranteed crash/data loss on valid input (e.g., `if is_admin or True:`); **`major`:** wrong business result or unhandled edge case on reachable inputs (e.g., dividing by `len(items)` before checking emptiness) |

> **Exam trap:** When a scenario shows developers ignoring an automated PR reviewer due to false positives, avoid answers that *"lower temperature to 0"*, *"tell the model to only report findings above 90% confidence"*, or *"keep all categories live while adding a disclaimer"*. Temporarily disable the noisy category and replace vague prompts with explicit report/skip criteria and severity examples.

---

## Few-Shot & Multishot Design

### When few-shot examples beat longer instructions
When prose rules are already clear yet outputs still vary in structure, tone, or boundary judgment, **2–5 targeted few-shot examples** (wrapped in `<examples><example>…</example></examples>`) are the highest-leverage intervention. Demonstrations teach **generalizable judgment** on novel patterns rather than brittle keyword matching on enumerated cases.

| Engineering goal | How to construct the `<example>` set |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Consistent output format** | Every example shows the complete target shape (for a ticket classifier: `intent`, `urgency`, `evidence_span`, `reply_draft`) with identical key order and casing |
| **False-positive suppression** | Use **contrast pairs**: one example showing a real defect that *is* reported alongside a plausible look-alike or valid repo idiom that produces `[]` (no finding) |
| **Ambiguous routing / tool choice** | Include a brief `<reasoning>` trace inside the example explaining *why* action A beats plausible alternative B |
| **Varied document extraction** | Demonstrate extraction across structural layouts (a prose paragraph with inline citations, a formal bibliography table, informal units like `"half a dozen"`, and a document missing an optional field returning `null`) |

### Structuring the example block
Keep demonstrations physically and semantically separate from the live request so the model never mistakes a sample input for the one it must process:

```xml
<examples>
  <example>
    <input>Card charged twice for order 5521</input>
    <ideal_output>{"intent": "billing", "urgency": "high"}</ideal_output>
  </example>
</examples>
<input>{{TICKET_TEXT}}</input>
```

* **Label the role of examples:** state that examples illustrate format and judgment only, and that names, amounts, and wording must come from the live `<input>`. Unlabeled examples get copied verbatim.
* **Show the target pattern, not the anti-pattern:** Gemini's prompt design guidance notes that examples of what to do steer better than examples of what to avoid. Contrast pairs still follow this rule: the look-alike input is paired with its *correct* (empty or benign) output.
* **Keep formatting identical across examples:** same tags, same key order, same whitespace conventions. Inconsistent demos teach inconsistent output.
* **Place examples in the static prefix:** examples before the live input stay cacheable and leave the task trigger at the end of the prompt.

### Preventing few-shot overfitting and bias
* **Randomize class order (class mixing):** listing four `"escalate"` examples followed by one `"resolve"` example biases the model toward escalating borderline inputs. Interleave outcomes and categories across examples.
* **Vary surface structure:** if every example invoice uses `USD` and three line items, the model may copy `USD` on a `EUR` document or drop a fourth line item. Vary lengths, field presence, and phrasings while keeping the schema invariant.
* **Demonstrate `null` explicitly:** to cure hallucination on missing required-looking fields, include at least one example where the source omits a field and the target output sets `"renewal_date": null` rather than guessing.

| Sample `<input_doc>` snippet | Target structured extraction | Boundary taught by the example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| *"Memo (14 May 2026): Pilot renewal approved for 18 months; PO number pending finance sign-off."* | `effective_date`: `"2026-05-14"`, `term_months`: `18`, `po_number`: `null`, `status`: `"approved"` | Normalizes informal prose dates to ISO-8601 while setting an explicitly pending field (`po_number`) to `null` |
| *"Verbal discussion notes — terms still under negotiation between legal teams; no dates agreed."* | `effective_date`: `null`, `term_months`: `null`, `po_number`: `null`, `status`: `"unclear"` | Demonstrates full `null` extraction plus the `"unclear"` escape hatch when no binding agreement exists |

---

## Reasoning, Effort & Sampling Controls

### Adaptive thinking and reasoning depth
Modern frontier models allocate variable test-time compute ("System 2" reasoning) before emitting visible output or between tool calls.

| Capability | Claude 4.6 / 4.7+ (`Messages API`) | Google Gemini (`Gemini API` / `Vertex AI`) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Enable reasoning** | `thinking={"type": "adaptive"}` (interleaves automatically across tool turns) | `thinking_config={"thinking_level": "HIGH"}` (model-dependent levels: `MINIMAL`, `LOW`, `MEDIUM`, `HIGH`) |
| **Control compute budget** | `output_config={"effort": "low" \| "medium" \| "high" \| "xhigh" \| "max"}` | `thinking_level` (or `thinking_budget` on earlier Gemini 2.5 models) |
| **Legacy trap** | Manual `{"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": N}` is deprecated on 4.6 and **returns HTTP 400 on Claude 4.7+** | Mixing legacy budget fields with level-based models fails validation |
| **Cost & latency rule** | Full internal thinking tokens are billed as output tokens even when `display: "omitted"`; use `low` effort for simple routers/classifiers | Thinking tokens count toward output billing and latency; dial down `thinking_level` on high-throughput classification |

### Sampling parameters and modern API constraints
* **Claude 4.7+ rejects non-default sampling parameters:** passing non-default `temperature`, `top_p`, or `top_k` on Claude 4.7+ returns an **HTTP 400** (and on earlier Claude 4.x models, `temperature` and `top_k` are incompatible with thinking). Frequency and presence penalties do not exist on the Claude API. Steer determinism and creativity through explicit criteria, few-shot examples, structured schemas, and `effort`.
* **Models that expose sampling (`Gemini`, open weights, older endpoints):** lower `temperature` (`0.0–0.2`) narrows token selection toward higher-probability paths for extraction and classification, while higher values (`0.7–1.0`) broaden diversity for brainstorming. Adjust `temperature` *or* `top_p`, rarely both simultaneously.
* **Low temperature is never a determinism guarantee:** floating-point batching, MoE routing, and hardware concurrency still produce run-to-run variation at `temperature=0`. Grade outputs on parsed schema properties and invariants, never exact raw string equality.
* **`max_tokens` / `max_output_tokens` is a hard cutoff, not a length instruction:** hitting the ceiling stops generation mid-token (`stop_reason == "max_tokens"` on Claude, `FinishReason.MAX_TOKENS` on Gemini), producing truncated, unparseable JSON. Ask for conciseness in the prompt/schema while sizing `max_tokens` with generous headroom.

### Reasoning prompt patterns (when explicit scaffolding helps)
* **Chain-of-Thought (CoT) in structured tasks:** when thinking mode is unavailable or disabled for latency, add a concise `"reasoning"` or `"evidence_quote"` string field *ahead* of classification fields in your schema so the model grounds its decision before committing to a label.
* **Contrastive examples:** show both a valid deduction and a common miscalculation (such as confusing fiscal-year dates with calendar-year dates) so the boundary is explicit.
* **Step-Back prompting:** ask the model to identify the governing policy principle or physical law first, then apply it to the specific case—useful when dense surface details obscure the rule.
* **Self-Consistency (majority voting):** sample multiple independent reasoning paths on hard, verifiable problems and aggregate the final structured answer—effective offline, too costly for low-latency chat.

---

## Decomposition & Prompt Chaining vs. Mega-Prompts

### Choosing the right decomposition strategy
Packing extraction, cross-reference verification, policy evaluation, and executive formatting into one giant "mega-prompt" dilutes attention across competing instructions and makes failures impossible to localize.

| Pattern | When to pick it | Concrete workflow example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Fixed sequential pipeline (prompt chaining)** | Stages and dependencies are known upfront; predictable multi-step transformation | **Step 1:** Extract normalized claims + dates per file → **Step 2:** Cross-check claims across files → **Step 3:** Render final compliance table |
| **Dynamic / adaptive decomposition** | Open-ended investigation where step `k+1` depends on what step `k` uncovers | Legacy test-suite expansion: map module graph → rank high-risk untested modules → inspect dependencies → adapt test plan as hidden couplings emerge |
| **Parallel fan-out + synthesis** | Independent inputs that need uniform local depth without cross-contaminating context | Summarize 25 customer-interview transcripts concurrently with one shared rubric, then run 1 synthesis call over their structured outputs |

### Iterative refinement patterns for engineering workflows
1. **Concrete input/output pairs over prose rewrites:** when prose instructions for a data transformation or formatting rule are interpreted inconsistently across edge cases, stop rephrasing adjectives—provide **2–3 concrete before/after input-output pairs** covering the tricky edge cases (such as `null` timestamps or nested arrays).
2. **Test-driven iteration:** write executable unit and edge-case tests first, run the model's implementation, and feed the exact failing test assertions back so each turn closes a verified gap.
3. **The interview pattern (clarify before building):** when designing in an unfamiliar domain or underspecified problem space, instruct the model to **ask targeted architectural questions first** (covering failure modes, cache invalidation, concurrency, state boundaries) before writing code or specs.
4. **Bundled vs. sequential bug feedback:** send **interacting** defects together in a single message so the fix accounts for shared state; fix **independent** defects sequentially so instructions stay focused.

---

## Structured Outputs & Schema Design

### Three ways to get structured data from a model

| Mechanism | Claude implementation | Gemini / Vertex AI implementation | Syntax guaranteed? | Best fit |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :---: | :--- |
| **1. Prompt-only formatting** | System/user prose or output style | System/user prose instructions | ❌ No | Streaming human-readable Markdown, YAML plans, UI prose |
| **2. Native JSON Schema output** | `output_config={"format": {"type": "json_schema", "schema": …}}` (or `claude -p --output-format json --json-schema`) | `GenerateContentConfig(response_mime_type="application/json", response_schema=…)` | ✅ Yes (on normal completion) | Single-step document extraction, classification, CI JSON gates |
| **3. Tool-use / function-call extraction** | `tools=[{…, "strict": True, "input_schema": …}]` + `tool_choice` | `tools=[FunctionDeclaration(…)]` + `FunctionCallingConfig` | ✅ Yes (with strict mode) | Multi-schema routing (`tool_choice: "any"`), agent pipelines, mandatory first-step extraction |

### Writing a schema-constrained output contract
A schema is part of the prompt: property names, enums, and `description` strings are all read by the model while constrained decoding enforces the shape.

```json
{"type": "object", "additionalProperties": false,
 "required": ["intent", "evidence_span", "urgency"],
 "properties": {
  "intent": {"type": "string", "enum": ["billing", "access", "bug", "other"]},
  "evidence_span": {"type": ["string", "null"], "description": "Verbatim quote that supports intent"},
  "urgency": {"type": "string", "enum": ["low", "high", "unclear"]}}}
```

* **Put field-level rules in `description`:** per-field extraction rules (*"verbatim quote"*, *"ISO-8601 date"*) sit next to the field; global policy stays in the system instruction.
* **One contract, not two:** never describe a JSON shape in prose with different key names from the schema. Conflicting contracts produce inconsistent fields when constraints are relaxed or the model changes.
* **Control property order where it matters:** Gemini's `response_schema` supports `propertyOrdering`; when a rationale or evidence field should be generated before the decision, order it first.
* **Shape is not truth:** a schema-valid object can still hold a wrong label or a quote that is not in the source, so keep the validation layer in place.

### Controlling tool selection with `tool_choice` / `FunctionCallingConfig`

| Mode | Claude `tool_choice` | Gemini `tool_config` mode | Behavior & production use case |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Auto** | `{"type": "auto"}` | `mode="AUTO"` | Model may return conversational text *or* call a tool. Default for multi-turn agents so the loop can end with `end_turn`. |
| **Any (must call a tool)** | `{"type": "any"}` | `mode="ANY"` (`allowed_function_names` optional) | Model **must** invoke one of the provided tools, choosing which schema fits. Ideal when routing an unknown document across `extract_invoice`, `extract_receipt`, and `extract_w9`. |
| **Forced named tool** | `{"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"}` | `mode="ANY"`, `allowed_function_names=["extract_metadata"]` | Model **must** call that exact tool. Use to guarantee a required first extraction step (`extract_metadata`) before downstream enrichment turns. |
| **None** | `{"type": "none"}` | `mode="NONE"` | Forbids tool calls while keeping tool definitions visible in context. |

> **Compatibility trap:** Forced tool selection (`"any"` or `"tool"`) is incompatible with manual extended thinking and is rejected on certain newer reasoning configurations; when forced mode is unavailable, pair `output_config.format` (for single schemas) or `tool_choice: "auto"` + `strict: true` + explicit prompt routing. Also remember to inspect `stop_reason` (`"end_turn"` / `"tool_use"` vs. `"refusal"` or `"max_tokens"`) before assuming a response satisfies your schema.

### Schema design rules that prevent hallucination

| Schema design decision | Anti-pattern | Production pattern | Why it matters |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Optional / missing source data** | Marking every property non-null `required` "for completeness" | Make potentially absent fields **nullable** (`"type": ["string", "null"]`) or optional, and state *"use `null` when not explicitly stated in the source"* | A non-null required field forces constrained decoding to **fabricate** a plausible date, PO number, or name when the document omits it |
| **Open-world categories** | Fixed enum `["billing", "technical", "shipping"]` | Fixed enum **plus `"other"`** paired with a nullable `"category_detail"` string | Preserves clean downstream aggregation without forcing novel cases into wrong buckets |
| **Genuine source ambiguity** | Binary enum `["approved", "rejected"]` | Add **`"unclear"`** (plus `"ambiguity_note"`) | Gives the model a truthful escape hatch when a contract draft is unsigned or contradictory |
| **Messy surface formats** | Relying on `"type": "string"` alone for dates/units | Keep `"type": ["string", "null"]` **and** put explicit normalization rules in the prompt (*"Convert all dates to ISO-8601 `YYYY-MM-DD`; convert weights to integer grams; strip currency symbols"*) | JSON Schema validates types (`string`, `number`), not how `"14/05/26"` vs. `"May 14"` was interpreted |
| **Strict-schema constraints** | Putting `minimum` / `maximum` or unbounded dicts into strict schemas | Set `"additionalProperties": false` on every object; enforce numeric ranges, cross-field sums, and regexes in application validator code | Strict constrained-decoding compilers support a subset of JSON Schema keywords and cap optional/union parameter counts; unsupported keywords return HTTP 400 |

---

## Validation, Retry & Dismissal Feedback Loops

### Syntax errors vs. semantic errors vs. absent information
Constrained JSON decoding (`output_config.format`, `strict: true`, `response_schema`) **eliminates syntax and type errors**—you will not get trailing commas, unquoted keys, or a string where a number was declared. It **never eliminates semantic errors**: line items that fail to sum to the invoice total, a shipping date copied into `invoice_date`, or two conflicting figures silently resolved by guessing.

| Failure class | Concrete example | Caught by strict schema? | Will retry-with-feedback fix it? | Correct system action |
| :--- | :--- | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| **Syntax / structural** | Truncated JSON, missing required key, string in float slot | ✅ Prevented upfront (unless `max_tokens` / `refusal`) | Yes (if not using strict mode) | Use strict schemas + check `stop_reason` |
| **Semantic / format mismatch** | `sum(line_items) == 940.00` while `stated_total == 1040.00`; date written `05/14/2026` instead of `2026-05-14` | ❌ No | ✅ **Yes** (1–2 bounded retries) | Re-prompt with original source + failed JSON + exact validator message |
| **Information absent from source** | Contract references *"Exhibit B pricing schedule"*, which was never uploaded | ❌ No | ❌ **No — retrying causes fabrication!** | Stop retrying; return `null`, fetch the missing exhibit, or route to human review |

### Designing self-verifying schemas and retry loops
* **Self-check fields in the extraction schema:**
  * **`stated_total` + `calculated_total`:** ask the model to extract the printed invoice total *and* compute/list individual line items so deterministic Python code checks `abs(sum(items) - stated_total) < 0.01` and flags discrepancies.
  * **`conflict_detected` (boolean) + `conflict_notes`:** when a multi-page packet states two different effective dates or revenue numbers, require the model to set `conflict_detected: true` and record both values rather than picking one silently.
* **Anatomy of a retry-with-error-feedback turn:** include (1) the **original source document**, (2) the **failed JSON extraction**, (3) the **exact programmatic validation error** (*"`line_items` sum to 410.00, which does not match `stated_total` 460.00; check whether a shipping or tax line was omitted"*), and (4) an explicit reminder to return `null` rather than guessing if the source genuinely lacks the figure. Cap retries at **1–2 attempts**.
* **Reviewer-override telemetry:** when a human reviewer corrects or rejects a model output, log the schema path of the overridden field, the prompt version, and one reason code from a fixed list (`wrong_field`, `missed_null`, `bad_normalization`, `not_in_source`). Aggregating overrides by field and reason code shows which instruction or example is ambiguous; fix it with a targeted contrast example and re-run the evaluation set before releasing the next prompt version.
* **Calibrating human review routing:** never disable human review based on a single aggregate metric (*"97% overall accuracy"* can hide 62% accuracy on handwritten amendments or `tax_id` fields). Slice accuracy by **document type × field**, have the model emit **field-level confidence** alongside `conflict_detected`, calibrate thresholds against a labeled validation set, route low-confidence or conflicting records to reviewers, and maintain **stratified random sampling** of high-confidence auto-approved extractions across every document type to catch drift and novel error modes.

---

## Batch Processing vs. Synchronous Execution

### Matching API transport to workflow latency and interactivity
Both Anthropic (**Message Batches API**) and Google Cloud (**Gemini / Vertex AI Batch Prediction**) offer asynchronous batch endpoints priced at **50% of synchronous token rates** with high throughput quotas and up to a **24-hour completion window**, with **no guaranteed per-request latency SLA**.

| Dimension | Synchronous API (`messages.create` / `generate_content`) | Asynchronous Batch API (`messages.batches` / Batch Prediction) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Pricing** | Standard input/output rates | **50% cost reduction** on input and output tokens |
| **Completion SLA** | Interactive (seconds); streaming supported | Up to **24 hours** (often faster, never guaranteed; unprocessed items expire at 24h) |
| **Multi-turn tool execution** | ✅ Supported: your loop executes tools between turns | ❌ **Single model turn per request:** cannot execute tools mid-request and feed `tool_result` back inside the same batch run |
| **Single-shot extraction via forced `tool_use`** | ✅ Supported | ✅ **Supported:** because the `tool_use` input block *is* the final structured record, no second turn is needed |
| **Result ordering & correlation** | Immediate 1:1 HTTP response | Out-of-order results; correlate every item via required **`custom_id`** |
| **Ideal workloads** | Live chat replies, interactive IDE assistance, agents that call tools between turns, any request a person is waiting on | Offline evaluation sweeps, product-catalog enrichment, back-filling labels on archived tickets, overnight log summarization |

### Prompt chaining across batch runs
Each batch request is a single model turn, so a multi-stage pipeline runs as a **chain of batches**: parse and validate stage *k* results in code, then embed them in the stage *k+1* requests.

| Stage | Request content | Hand-off to the next stage |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1. Extract** (batch) | System prompt + `<document>` + JSON schema | Parsed records keyed by `custom_id` |
| **2. Validate** (code, no model call) | Schema parse, cross-field checks | Valid records forward; failures to a retry batch or review queue |
| **3. Synthesize** (batch or sync) | Validated records inside `<extracted_records>` + task instruction | Final summary or report |

* **Hand off structured data inside named tags:** pass validated JSON in `<extracted_records>` and instruct the next stage to rely only on that block. Re-sending the raw source alongside invites the model to re-extract and contradict stage 1.
* **Version each stage prompt separately:** a chain localizes failures only if every stage has its own template, schema, and evaluation set.
* **Dry-run request bodies synchronously:** send a handful of representative requests through the Messages API first; a malformed request only shows up as an `errored` result after the batch has run.
* **Correlate by meaningful `custom_id`:** results arrive in any order. Use ids that encode record and stage (`tkt-88412-s1`); resend `expired` items as they are, and fix the request before resending `errored` ones.

> **Design note:** Batch fits work nobody is actively waiting on. When a person or a downstream gate blocks on the result, stay synchronous (with prompt caching for the shared prefix) regardless of the discount.

---

## Multi-Instance & Multi-Pass Review Architectures

### Chain-of-thought isolation: keep reasoning out of the answer
Reasoning improves hard decisions, but downstream code and end users should consume only the final result. Give reasoning its own channel and parse only the answer channel.

| Mechanism | How reasoning is separated | What your code consumes |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Prompted CoT** (thinking mode off) | Instruct the model to reason inside `<thinking>` and place the result inside `<answer>` | Only the `<answer>` contents; log `<thinking>` for debugging |
| **Claude extended / adaptive thinking** | The response carries `thinking` content blocks separate from `text` and `tool_use` blocks | The `text` or `tool_use` blocks, selected by block type |
| **Gemini thinking** | Thoughts stay internal; with `include_thoughts` enabled, thought summaries arrive as parts flagged `thought` | Parts not flagged as thoughts |
| **Schema field** | A short `rationale` property ordered before the decision fields | The decision fields; `rationale` is audit text, never data |

* **Why isolate:** reasoning text leaking ahead of JSON breaks parsers, exposes scratch work to users, and can echo untrusted input back into downstream systems.
* **Never demand both "think step by step" and bare JSON:** without a dedicated channel the model either skips the reasoning or pollutes the output. Enable thinking, add a tag pair, or add a schema field.
* **Grade answers, not explanations:** a fluent rationale is not proof of a correct decision; evaluate the parsed answer against labeled data.

### Multi-pass critique chains

| Pattern | Context given to the checking call | Best fit |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Same-session "check your work"** *(weak)* | Full generation history | Catching obvious slips only; the model tends to defend its own earlier reasoning |
| **Draft → critique → revise chain** | Critique call receives the draft and rubric; revise call receives draft plus critique | Raising quality while logging every intermediate output |
| **Independent grader instance** | Fresh context with only the artifact, source, and rubric | Grounding and policy checks free of the generator's assumptions |
| **Multi-sample agreement** | Several independent samples of the same task | Verifiable answers (labels, numbers) where agreement signals reliability |

1. **Draft** with the stage-1 prompt and store the output.
2. **Critique** in a separate call containing `<draft>`, `<source>`, and `<rubric>`; return a schema list of issues (`criterion`, `quote`, `fix`).
3. **Revise** in a third call that receives the draft and the issue list and returns the result inside `<answer>` or a schema.
4. **Stop deterministically:** end after 1–2 rounds or when the critique returns an empty list, and keep every stage in the trace for evaluation.

---

## Prompt Caching, Security & Enterprise LLMOps

### Prefix ordering for prompt caching
Both Claude (`cache_control`) and Gemini (implicit and explicit context caching) match caches on **exact byte-for-byte prefixes**. Changing a timestamp, user name, or tool schema near the top of a prompt invalidates everything beneath it.

| Position in request | Content | Mutability |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1. Top (Prefix)** | Tool definitions → system instructions → normalization rubrics → `<examples>` → shared reference corpus | Static across calls (**cached**) |
| **2. Middle** | Session history / prior turns (with incremental cache breakpoints) | Append-only across turns |
| **3. Bottom (Suffix)** | Current document, PR diff, per-request variables, and final task query | Changes every call (**uncached**) |

* **Claude cache economics:** 5-minute TTL writes cost **1.25×** base input tokens (break-even after **1** cache read at ~**0.1×**); 1-hour TTL writes cost **2×** base input tokens (break-even after **2** reads). Keep `thinking` / `effort` settings stable within a workload so message-history caches stay warm.

### Defending prompts against untrusted inputs
* **Prompts are not security boundaries:** a clever indirect prompt injection inside a parsed PDF or PR description can urge the model to ignore instructions or call a destructive tool.
* **Defense-in-depth stack:** (1) isolate untrusted text inside explicit XML tags (`<untrusted_pr_body>…</untrusted_pr_body>`) and instruct the model to treat tag contents strictly as data; (2) restrict agent tool sets to least privilege (`Read`, `Grep`, `Glob` only on untrusted review runs); and (3) enforce deterministic policy checks (refund thresholds, allowed file paths, schema validation) in **application code or `PreToolUse` hooks**, never solely in prose.

### Prompt versioning, automated optimization, and when to fine-tune
* **Treat prompts and schemas as versioned code:** store prompt templates, JSON schemas, model IDs (pinned snapshots such as `claude-sonnet-4-6`), and `effort` / `thinking_level` configs in version control gated by regression evals ([AgentOps](https://mbettan.github.io/machine-learning-cert/AgentOps.html#grading-hierarchy)).
* **Automated prompt optimization (APE / Vertex AI Prompt Optimizer):** once you have a labeled golden dataset and programmatic metric (schema F1, per-category precision), optimizer loops can systematically mutate instructions and select few-shot examples to lift accuracy—especially when migrating between model families.
* **Prompting vs. Fine-Tuning (SFT / LoRA):**

| Lever | Changes weights? | Reach for it when… | Avoid it when… |
| :--- | :---: | :--- | :--- |
| **Prompting + Few-Shot + Schema** | ❌ No | Iterating rapidly, enforcing JSON structure, reasoning over fresh context/RAG, low-to-medium volume | Prompt prefix exceeds latency/cost budgets on millions of identical narrow calls |
| **Retrieval (RAG) / Context** | ❌ No | Facts change daily or require source citations and per-user ACLs | You only need consistent output formatting or tone |
| **Supervised Fine-Tuning / LoRA** | ✅ Yes | Distilling a large teacher model's specialized style/classification into a small fast SLM at massive scale | Trying to teach rapidly changing facts or compensate for missing schema validation |

---

## Failure Modes & Diagnostic Traps

| Observed production symptom | Root cause | Correct engineering fix | Tempting wrong answer |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Ticket-triage model marks 40% of tickets `urgent`; support agents stop trusting the flag | `urgent` is defined only as *"time-sensitive"*, with no boundary | Define urgency with explicit criteria (outage, security exposure, payment blocked) plus contrast examples of look-alike non-urgent tickets | Asking the model to *"only mark urgent when very confident"* |
| Extractor invents `"1970-01-01"` or plausible dates when contracts omit `renewal_date` | `renewal_date` is non-null `required` in the JSON schema | Make `renewal_date` nullable (`["string", "null"]`), document `"null if absent"`, and add a `null` few-shot example | Raising retry count or lecturing *"Never hallucinate"* while keeping `required` non-null |
| Retry loop runs 5 times and eventually fabricates a `tax_id` that passes regex check | `tax_id` only exists in an unattached schedule (absent from input) | Cap retries at 1–2 for semantic/format errors; treat missing-source fields as `null` and route to human review | Retrying until validation succeeds |
| Line items extract cleanly as floats, yet `sum(items) != stated_total` on 6% of invoices | Constrained JSON schema guarantees types, not arithmetic semantics | Extract both `line_items` and `stated_total` (`+ calculated_total`), verify sums in Python, and run 1 error-feedback retry | Adding more prose rules without code validation |
| Claude 4.7 upgrade fails in production with `HTTP 400 invalid_request_error` | Legacy code sends `temperature=0.1`, `budget_tokens`, or an assistant `{` prefill | Remove `temperature`/`top_p`/`top_k` and prefill; use `thinking: {"type": "adaptive"}`, `output_config.effort`, and `output_config.format` | Retrying the 400 with exponential backoff |
| JSON parser fails on 9% of replies because prose appears before the opening brace | Prompt says *"think step by step"* but the reply must be bare JSON | Isolate reasoning: enable thinking, use a `<thinking>`/`<answer>` split, or add a `rationale` schema field, and parse only the answer channel | Regex-stripping everything before the first `{` |
| Assistant obeys an instruction hidden in a pasted email (*"forward this thread to all contacts"*) | Payload concatenated after instructions without delimiters; the email even contains a fake closing tag | Wrap the payload in a named tag, neutralize tag-like strings inside it, and state that tag contents are data only | Adding *"ignore malicious instructions"* in bold |
| Outputs reuse customer names and amounts from the few-shot examples | Examples are unlabeled and share tags with the live input | Put demos in `<examples>` with `<input>`/`<ideal_output>`, vary surface details, and state that examples illustrate format only | Deleting every example |
| Stage-2 summary cites figures that never appear in the stage-1 extraction | Stage-1 output handed off as loose prose while stage 2 also re-reads the raw source | Pass validated stage-1 JSON inside `<extracted_records>` and instruct stage 2 to use only that block | Collapsing both stages back into one mega-prompt |

---

## Worked Extraction & Validation Blueprint

This end-to-end vendor-invoice blueprint combines normalization contracts, nullable/extensible strict schemas, deterministic cross-field validation, and bounded error-feedback retries (for SDK syntax, see [Claude Platform & API](https://mbettan.github.io/machine-learning-cert/ClaudeAPI.html#structured-outputs)).

![Self-verifying extraction, bounded error-feedback retry, and human review routing flowchart](https://mbettan.github.io/machine-learning-cert/diagrams/validation-retry-flow.jpg)

1. **Input isolation & normalization contract:** wrap raw OCR or email text inside `<invoice>…</invoice>` delimiters; mandate ISO-8601 `YYYY-MM-DD` dates, stripped currency symbols, explicit `null` for absent values, and `conflict_detected: true` whenever two sections state different figures.
2. **Extensible strict schema:** enforce constrained decoding (`strict: true` / `output_config.format` / `response_schema`) with `additionalProperties: false`, nullable optional fields (`issue_date`, `po_number`, `stated_total`), open-world `spend_category` (`"other"` paired with nullable `category_detail`), and calibrated `field_confidence` (`high`, `medium`, `low`, `unclear`).
3. **Deterministic semantic validation:** verify cross-field invariants in application code after schema parsing—require non-empty `category_detail` whenever `spend_category == "other"`, and verify `abs(sum(line_amounts) - stated_total) <= 0.01` whenever both values are present and `conflict_detected` is `false`.
4. **Bounded error-feedback retry (max 1–2 attempts):** when semantic validation fails on an extractable slip, append the failed record and exact validator error (`is_error: true`, e.g., *"line_amounts sum to 410.00 vs. stated_total 460.00; re-check omitted tax/shipping lines or set conflict_detected=true"*) while reminding the model to keep `null` rather than guessing missing facts.
5. **Calibrated human routing & stratified audit:** bypass retries and route directly to a human review queue whenever `stop_reason` is unexpected (`max_tokens`, `refusal`), `conflict_detected` is `true`, calibrated `field_confidence` is `low`/`unclear`, or the retry cap expires—and continuously audit a stratified random sample of verified records across every document type.

---

## Glossary

| Term | Definition |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Adaptive Thinking** | Dynamic test-time reasoning mode (`thinking: {"type": "adaptive"}`) scaled via `output_config.effort`, replacing fixed `budget_tokens`. |
| **Attention dilution** | Recall drop caused by packing too many documents, rules, or tasks into one prompt; cured by splitting work into focused chained or parallel calls. |
| **Chain-of-thought isolation** | Giving reasoning its own channel (thinking blocks, `<thinking>` tags, or a `rationale` field) so code parses only the final answer. |
| **Class mixing** | Interleaving target labels across few-shot examples so the model does not over-predict whichever class appeared first or last. |
| **Constrained decoding** | Token-level grammar masking (`output_config.format`, `strict: true`, `response_schema`) that guarantees schema-valid JSON syntax. |
| **Contrast pair** | Two few-shot examples pairing a genuine positive case with a near-miss acceptable case that should *not* be flagged. |
| **`custom_id`** | Per-request correlation string in Batch APIs used to match out-of-order results and resubmit only failed items. |
| **Independent review instance** | Separate model call with clean context (artifact + rubric only) that avoids anchoring on the generator's reasoning trace. |
| **Interview pattern** | Prompting the model to ask clarifying architectural and edge-case questions before generating an implementation. |
| **Lost in the Middle** | U-shaped positional recall effect where models attend strongly to prompt start and end while missing details buried mid-window. |
| **Nullable schema field** | Property typed `["string", "null"]` (or optional) so the model outputs `null` rather than fabricating data absent from the source. |
| **Prompt chaining** | Splitting a task into sequential calls whose validated outputs are passed to the next stage inside named tags. |
| **Retry with error feedback** | Bounded follow-up turn supplying the source, failed extraction, and exact validator error so the model repairs semantic/format slips. |
| **Semantic validation error** | Output that parses against the JSON schema yet violates domain invariants (e.g., line items not summing to `stated_total`). |
| **Stratified random sampling** | Ongoing human audit sampling across every document type and field stratum—including high-confidence auto-approved outputs—to measure true error rates. |
| **`tool_choice`** | Parameter (`auto`, `any`, forced `tool`, `none`) controlling whether the model may or must invoke a tool on the current turn. |
| **XML tag delimiting** | Wrapping each content type in consistently named tags so instructions, examples, and untrusted input stay unambiguous. |

# Agentic Design Patterns (ADP): Study Guide

> **Author:** Michaël Bettan  
> **Version:** 1.0

---

## 00. Overview & Mental Model

**Definition:** Agentic design patterns are reusable, vendor-neutral architectural blueprints that govern how an LLM-based system decomposes work, selects control flow, invokes tools, manages context memory, coordinates across specialized workers, and defers high-stakes decisions to deterministic code or human reviewers. They apply identically across Google ADK, the Claude Agent SDK, LangGraph, or direct model API loops.

**What agentic design patterns solve for:** A raw language model is a stateless, probabilistic token predictor—it can *propose* an action, but it cannot *execute* tools, enforce hard business invariants, persist session state, or halt a runaway loop. Architectural patterns define **who owns the control flow** (deterministic application code vs. dynamic model reasoning), **where authority sits** (code gates vs. model judgment vs. human sign-off), and **how context stays clean** as tasks scale.

> **Mental model:**  
> The model is the **probabilistic reasoning engine**; the architecture is the **deterministic harness** (nervous system, brakes, and safety interlocks) that decides when the model thinks, when tools execute, and when a human must approve.

> **Rule 0 (The Simplicity Ladder):**  
> **Start with the simplest architecture that passes your evaluation suite.** Climb from deterministic code $\rightarrow$ a single augmented LLM call $\rightarrow$ a predefined workflow $\rightarrow$ an autonomous agent **only when empirical evaluations prove the simpler tier fails.**

### LLM vs. Workflow vs. Autonomous Agent vs. Harness

| Layer | Control Owner | Role & Runtime Behavior | Memory Hook |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Raw LLM** | Caller (1 turn) | Stateless token predictor; reasons over prompt context and emits text or structured tool requests, but never executes code. | *"Brain in a jar"* |
| **Augmented LLM** | Caller (1 turn + tools) | Single model call equipped with **Retrieval** (RAG), **Tools** (MCP/functions), and **Memory** (read/write state). Handles most production features. | *"LLM with a backpack"* |
| **Composable Workflow** | **Application code** | Multi-step pipeline where LLMs and tools execute along **predefined code paths** with deterministic gates between steps. | *"Railway tracks"* — train cannot leave the rails |
| **Autonomous Agent** | **The model** | LLM dynamically directs its own multi-turn process, choosing which tools to call and when to stop based on environmental ground truth. | *"Taxi"* — driver picks the route dynamically |
| **Agent Harness / Framework** | Infrastructure | Runtime layer (ADK, Claude Agent SDK, LangGraph) supplying the event loop, state persistence, sandboxing, callbacks, and observability. | *"Chassis, brakes & dashboard"* |

> [!WARNING]
> **Classic architectural trap:** Calling an LLM five times in a Python script does **not** make the system an "autonomous agent." If application code dictates the sequence, branching, and retry count, it is a **workflow**. It becomes an **agent** only when the model itself decides the next step and action trajectory at runtime.

---

## 01. Architectural Triage & Sequential Decision Framework (`#triage-decomposition`)

Before writing a single system prompt or selecting an orchestration framework, an architect must resolve four sequential decisions. Skipping step 1 or 2 is the primary cause of over-engineered, brittle, or unsafe agentic deployments.

### Sequential Architectural Decision Framework

```
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Stage 1: Problem Decomposition & Execution Engine Triage                   │
│   └─► Triage every sub-task across Tripartite Execution Regimes            │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Stage 2: Work-Shape Selection                                              │
│   └─► Single Augmented Call vs. Composable Workflow vs. Autonomous Agent   │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Stage 3: Execution Routing, Model Tiering & Hosting Infrastructure         │
│   └─► Model tier routing (fast vs. frontier), sync/stream/batch, residency │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Stage 4: Guardrail Wrapping, Invariant Verification & Human-in-the-Loop    │
│   └─► Pre-LLM epistemic gates, tool-boundary hooks, auditors, HITL gates   │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

1. **Stage 1 — Problem Decomposition & Execution Engine Triage:** Separate the problem into deterministic rules, probabilistic reasoning, and human accountability using the **Tripartite Execution Regimes** below.
2. **Stage 2 — Work-Shape Selection:** Select the lowest rung on the complexity ladder (Single Call $\rightarrow$ Workflow $\rightarrow$ Autonomous Agent) using the **Architectural Evaluation Criteria** (§02).
3. **Stage 3 — Execution Routing, Model Tiering & Hosting Infrastructure:** Match each step to the right model tier and reasoning effort (e.g., high-capability planner producing a spec for a fast/balanced executor), transport mode (streaming vs. async batch), and regional data boundary.
4. **Stage 4 — Guardrail Wrapping, Invariant Verification & Human-in-the-Loop Controls:** Surround every probabilistic step with deterministic pre-checks, schema validators, tool-boundary hooks, independent critique, and Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) checkpoints.

### Tripartite Execution Regimes: Deterministic Code, Probabilistic Inference & Human Oversight

Every enterprise workflow is a hybrid of three distinct execution regimes. Never assign Regime 1 or Regime 3 responsibilities to Regime 2:

| Execution Regime | Execution Engine | What Belongs Here | Canonical Examples | Why Other Regimes Fail |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Regime 1: Deterministic Code** | Plain application code, SQL, regex, type schemas, policy hooks | Exact arithmetic, schema validation, RBAC & permission enforcement, idempotency keys, database writes, PII redaction, hard policy gates | Fee & tax calculations, date math, checking `amount <= 500`, enforcing `user_id` tenant scoping, verifying cited section headers exist in source text | LLMs introduce **deterministic invariant degradation** (silent tail-risk arithmetic or rule violations); humans are too slow and inconsistent at scale |
| **Regime 2: Probabilistic Model (LLM)** | Augmented LLM, Workflow node, or Agent loop | Unstructured synthesis, semantic classification, ambiguous entity extraction, fuzzy matching, multi-step planning over open-ended inputs | Summarizing conflicting legal clauses, triaging free-text support tickets, diagnosing novel stack traces across a codebase, drafting code diffs | Rigid code/regex shatters on phrasing variations; humans cannot manually read 50,000 documents per hour |
| **Regime 3: Human-in-the-Loop (HITL)** | Human reviewer via durable approval queue / UI checkpoint | High-blast-radius irreversible actions, novel policy exceptions, regulated sign-offs, subjective value trade-offs | Approving a `$25,000` wire refund, executing a production database drop, granting an exception to legal policy, merging security-critical PRs | Code lacks contextual judgment for novel exceptions; models cannot bear legal, financial, or ethical accountability |

### Hard Invariant Enforcement in Code (Preventing Deterministic Drift)

**Deterministic drift** occurs when an engineering team delegates exact, rule-bound logic—such as calculating pro-rated subscription refunds, enforcing role-based access control (RBAC), checking date eligibility windows, or redacting Social Security Numbers—to a system prompt instead of application code.

- **Why it is dangerous:** Even when a frontier model follows a prompt rule on the vast majority of test runs, probabilistic token sampling guarantees a non-zero tail-risk failure rate—especially under **instruction crowding** (long prompts with 20+ competing rules) or adversarial prompt injection.
- **Architectural rule ("Deterministic Handcuffs"):** Let the LLM extract structured parameters or propose an action, but execute all math, eligibility comparisons, permission checks, and compliance gates in **deterministic code** (`PreToolUse` / `before_tool_callback` hooks, Pydantic validators, or SQL constraints).

---

## 02. Work-Shape Spectrum & Architectural Evaluation Criteria (`#work-shape-matrix`)

Once Regime 2 (the probabilistic work) is isolated, choose between the three primary work shapes: **Single Augmented LLM Call**, **Composable Workflow**, and **Autonomous Agent**.

### Architectural Evaluation Criteria: Single Call vs. Workflow vs. Autonomous Agent

| Evaluation Criterion | Single Augmented LLM Call | Composable Workflow (DAG / Chain) | Autonomous Agent (Open Loop) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1. Task Path Predictability** | **Fully known (1 step):** Input maps directly to output with retrieved context or a single tool lookup. | **Known decomposition ($K$ steps):** Multi-step process where the sequence, branches, or fan-out categories are fixed in advance. | **Unknown / emergent ($N$ steps):** Step $N+1$ depends entirely on what tool observation $N$ revealed (e.g., debugging an unknown bug). |
| **2. Latency Budget** | **Sub-second to ~3 s:** Single model roundtrip; suitable for synchronous inline UI responses. | **~3 s to ~15 s:** Predictable bounded latency ($K$ sequential stages or $1$ parallel fan-out + join). | **Seconds to minutes+:** Open-ended $O(N)$ sequential turns; requires async streaming, progress UI, or background execution. |
| **3. Error Blast Radius & Reversibility** | **Low / read-only:** Output is displayed to a user or validated by a caller before any state mutation. | **Medium / gated:** Intermediate code gates catch errors between stages before downstream side-effects run. | **High if ungated:** Multi-turn tool mutations can compound; requires sandboxing, checkpoints, and HITL gates on writes. |
| **4. Token Cost Ceiling** | **~1× baseline:** Minimal prompt overhead; highest prompt-cache hit ratio. | **~3–5× baseline:** Bounded multiplier across $K$ focused prompts; easy to route cheap tiers to simple nodes. | **~10–15×+ baseline:** Context accumulates across turns and tool outputs; requires strict token/turn caps and compaction. |
| **5. Auditability & Compliance Rigor** | **High:** Single input/output pair; trivial to log and reproduce. | **Highest for multi-step:** Deterministic transitions and explicit code gate pass/fail logs satisfy strict regulatory audits. | **Complex:** Nondeterministic trajectories require full event-ledger tracing (`tool_trajectory`) and replay harnesses. |

### Inherent Operating Characteristics of Probabilistic Systems

Every agentic architecture must explicitly defend against four inherent properties of language models:

1. **Non-determinism:** Identical prompts can yield different phrasings or tool trajectories across runs (and modern frontier APIs reject non-default sampling knobs like `temperature: 0` or still exhibit floating-point variance). *Mitigation:* Grade structured properties and behavioral rubrics, never exact string equality; enforce JSON schemas at the token level.
2. **Plausible-sounding errors (Hallucinations & Silent Corruption):** Models are trained to complete patterns helpfully. When fed garbled OCR text, an empty string `""` from a timed-out tool, or a missing policy clause, an unguarded model will invent confident facts or fabricated citations (`Section 99.1`). *Mitigation:* Pre-LLM epistemic quality gates, explicit `is_error: true` tool results, and deterministic citation verification against source text.
3. **Context sensitivity (Attention Dilution & Instruction Crowding):** Packing 30 rules, 15 irrelevant documents, and 40 tool schemas into one call degrades recall in the middle of the window and causes the model to silently drop late audit rules. *Mitigation:* Split generation from verification, keep tool catalogs $\le 16$ tools per agent, and isolate noisy exploration in subagents.
4. **Compounding multi-step error rates:** If a single autonomous step has a $95\%$ reliability rate, a 10-step unverified chain succeeds only $0.95^{10} \approx 60\%$ of the time, because an early misread file or wrong assumption poisons every subsequent reasoning turn. *Mitigation:* Insert **ground-truth environmental feedback** (compilers, unit tests, schema validators, deterministic gates) after every step to reset the error curve.

---

## 03. The 5 Canonical Workflow Patterns

When a single call falls short because of instruction crowding, multi-stage dependencies, or latency/cost constraints—but the overall control structure is predictable—use one or more of the **five composable workflow patterns**. In all five, **application code owns the control flow** (or bounds the loop).

| Pattern | Control Flow Shape | Primary Optimization | Canonical Use Case | Memory Hook |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1. Prompt Chaining** | `LLM 1 ──► [Code Gate] ──► LLM 2 ──► LLM 3` | Accuracy via focused sub-steps + early fail-fast | Drafting an outline $\rightarrow$ verifying structure in code $\rightarrow$ generating full localized report | *"Assembly line with quality inspectors"* |
| **2. Routing** | `Classifier ──► Specialist Handler A | B | C` | Separation of concerns & per-tier cost optimization | Directing billing, refund, and tech-support tickets to distinct prompts, tools, and model tiers | *"Hospital triage desk"* |
| **3. Parallelization** | `Fan-Out (N calls) ──► Programmatic Aggregator` | Wall-clock speed (*Sectioning*) or high confidence (*Voting*) | Running content safety screening in parallel with answer generation (*Sectioning*); multi-prompt code security audit (*Voting*) | *"Sectioning = slice the pizza; Voting = poll 5 judges"* |
| **4. Orchestrator–Workers** | `Orchestrator LLM ──► Dynamic Workers (1..K) ──► Synthesizer` | Runtime task decomposition when sub-tasks depend on input | Multi-file refactoring or multi-source research where the target files/sources aren't known upfront | *"Tech lead assigning tickets after reading the spec"* |
| **5. Evaluator–Optimizer** | `Generator ──► Critic/Auditor ──► (Pass | Feedback Loop [max M])` | Iterative quality & compliance against a strict rubric | Legal clause extraction + adversarial citation auditor; literary translation refinement | *"Writer + strict editor"* |

### Pattern 1: Prompt Chaining (Sequential Pipeline with Code Gates)

Decomposes a complex task into a fixed sequence of narrower LLM calls, where each step consumes the validated output of the previous step.

| Pipeline Stage | Component | Functionality | Invariant / Exit Condition |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Step 1: Extraction** | Extraction LLM | Extracts structured clauses and cited line anchors from source text. | Emits structured JSON matching schema. |
| **Deterministic Code Gate** | Application Code | Validates mandatory fields (`termination_clause`) and citations list. | If missing or invalid, halts execution immediately ($0 downstream spend). |
| **Step 2: Risk Assessment** | Assessment LLM | Analyzes validated clauses against risk rubrics. | Emits final structured risk assessment report. |

- **The Gate (`gate_check`):** Always insert a deterministic code check (schema validation, regex citation lookup, length/completeness check) between steps so corrupted intermediate outputs fail fast for `$0` rather than poisoning downstream calls.
- **When NOT to use:** Do not chain steps that have no data dependency (use *Parallelization* instead to avoid serial latency) or tasks that a single well-structured prompt already solves cleanly.

### Pattern 2: Routing (Intent & Complexity Dispatch)

Classifies an incoming request (via a fast small model, embedding similarity, or deterministic rules) and dispatches it to a specialized prompt, scoped toolset, or appropriate model tier.

- **Why routing beats a monolith prompt:** Optimizing a single mega-prompt to handle billing disputes, technical debugging, and account cancellations simultaneously causes instruction clash and forces every call to pay for the largest model tier and full tool catalog.
- **Model-tier routing:** Route high-volume, routine intents to a fast, low-cost tier (e.g., Haiku / Gemini Flash-Lite) with minimal reasoning effort, and reserve frontier tiers (Sonnet / Opus / Gemini Pro) for complex multi-step troubleshooting.
- **Preventing misrouting cascades:** Include an explicit `unclear / ambiguous` fallback category that asks a clarifying question or routes to a general handler, log confidence scores, and validate that the target handler rejects out-of-domain requests rather than guessing.

### Pattern 3: Parallelization (Sectioning vs. Voting)

Executes multiple LLM calls concurrently (`asyncio.gather` / `ParallelAgent`) and merges their outputs programmatically or via a downstream synthesizer.

| Variant | Architecture | Goal | Key Engineering Rule |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Sectioning** | Split a task into **distinct, independent subtasks** or personas run concurrently. | **Speed & focused attention:** Total latency equals the slowest branch rather than the sum of branches. | Keep each branch's output key isolated (`output_key="market"`, `output_key="pricing"`) so concurrent workers never overwrite shared mutable state. Running guardrails/PII screening in parallel with response generation avoids adding serial latency. |
| **Voting** | Run the **same task multiple times** (either identical prompt at $T>0$ for *Self-Consistency CoT*, or diverse critique prompts) and aggregate via threshold/majority vote. | **High confidence & recall:** Reduces false negatives on high-stakes reviews. | Tune the vote threshold to match asymmetric risk: e.g., in a security vulnerability scan, flag the diff if **any 1 of 3** reviewers finds an exploit (high recall); in noisy classification, require **2 of 3** agreement (high precision). |

### Pattern 4: Orchestrator–Workers (Dynamic Task Decomposition)

A central **Orchestrator LLM** inspects the input, dynamically invents a list of subtasks (because the exact number and nature of subtasks cannot be hardcoded in advance), dispatches **Worker LLMs** with scoped context, and synthesizes their returned summaries.

- **Orchestrator–Workers vs. Parallelization:** Both fan out work to multiple calls, but in **Parallelization** the branches are **predefined in code** (e.g., always run Financial, Legal, and Technical checks), whereas in **Orchestrator–Workers** the branches are **determined dynamically at runtime by the orchestrator model** (e.g., inspecting a bug report and deciding which 4 out of 2,000 repository files need targeted worker edits).
- **Spec-Driven Planner $\rightarrow$ Executor split:** A high-capability model acts as the read-only orchestrator/planner to resolve ambiguities and emit a structured task specification, then dispatches mid-tier or fast-tier workers in fresh context windows to execute each bounded subtask.

| Orchestration Phase | Execution Engine | Mechanism | Guardrail |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Phase 1: Dynamic Decomposition** | Orchestrator LLM | Generates structured task plan based on runtime input inspection. | Strict Pydantic task schema (`subtasks: list[SubTask]`). |
| **Phase 2: Scoped Worker Fan-Out** | Parallel Worker LLMs | Workers execute bounded subtasks in fresh, isolated context windows. | Bounded concurrency waves (3–5 workers max) with private outputs. |
| **Phase 3: Context Synthesis** | Synthesizer LLM | Merges worker `HandoffContract` summaries into unified deliverable. | Artifact pointer pattern: large diffs stay on disk/storage. |

### Pattern 5: Evaluator–Optimizer (Bounded Generator–Critic Loop)

Pairs a **Generator** call with an independent **Evaluator / Critic** call that grades the draft against an explicit rubric and returns actionable revision feedback in a loop.

- **Two prerequisites for fit:** (1) Output quality measurably improves when a human provides structured feedback, and (2) an LLM (paired with deterministic checks) can reliably articulate that feedback.
- **Separation of Authority (Avoiding Self-Grading Bias):** Never ask the same prompt in the same turn to both draft an answer and grade its own compliance—it will rationalize its own mistakes. Use a separate critic call with a cold context (`include_contents='none'`), an adversarial rubric prompt, and deterministic verification tools (e.g., checking that every cited clause actually appears in the source document).
- **Mandatory loop hygiene:** Always enforce `max_iterations` (typically 2–3 rounds) and an explicit convergence/exit signal (`escalate=True` / `status="approved"`). If `max_iterations` trips without passing the rubric, do **not** silently ship the unverified draft—mark the state unapproved and escalate to HITL or a safe fallback.

| Loop Phase | Agent / Mechanism | Inputs & Context | Exit / Escalation Criteria |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Generation** | Generator LLM | Task brief + prior critic feedback (if any). | Emits structured draft with cited section headers. |
| **Pre-Critic Gate** | Deterministic Code | Source text + draft citations. | Deterministically checks that cited headers exist in source text; fails fast if missing. |
| **Evaluation** | Cold-Context Critic LLM | Source text + draft + rubric (`include_contents='none'`). | Emits `approved: bool` and actionable critique. Loop terminates if `approved == True`. |
| **Termination / Fallback** | Deterministic Guard | Iteration counter (`attempt <= max_iterations`). | If `attempt > max_iterations` without approval, fails closed to HITL escalation. |

### Cross-Vendor Pattern Vocabulary

| Architectural Pattern | Anthropic / General Framing | Google Cloud / ADK Primitive | Graph / State Machine Framing |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Single Building Block** | Augmented LLM (Retrieval + Tools + Memory) | `LlmAgent` with `tools` + `MemoryService` | Single node with tool bindings |
| **Pattern 1: Sequential** | Prompt Chaining + Programmatic Gate | `SequentialAgent` / `Workflow` + `before_agent_callback` | Linear edges + conditional gate node |
| **Pattern 2: Dispatch** | Routing (Intent / Tier Classifier) | Coordinator (`sub_agents`) or custom router node | Conditional edge router from `START` |
| **Pattern 3a: Split Work** | Parallelization — Sectioning | `ParallelAgent` (distinct `output_key`s) + synthesizer | Fan-out branches $\rightarrow$ `JoinNode` |
| **Pattern 3b: Consensus** | Parallelization — Voting / Self-Consistency | `ParallelAgent` ($N\times$ runs) + vote aggregator | Parallel ensemble $\rightarrow$ majority/threshold reducer |
| **Pattern 4: Dynamic** | Orchestrator–Workers | `LlmAgent` invoking specialist `AgentTool`s | Dynamic map-reduce / send API |
| **Pattern 5: Refinement** | Evaluator–Optimizer | `LoopAgent(max_iterations=N)` + generator & critic | Cyclic edge bounded by iteration counter |
| **Open-Ended Autonomy** | Autonomous Agent (Tools in a Loop) | `LlmAgent` native ReAct loop (`Runner`) | Cyclic `agent` $\rightleftarrows$ `tools` graph |
| **Human Checkpoint** | Planned Checkpoint / HITL Approval | `FunctionTool(..., require_confirmation=True)` | `interrupt()` / `RequestInput` with checkpointer |
